text:
Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with a fixed number of binary digits. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding a to b and then adding c is equivalent to adding a to the sum of b and c. Floating-point arithmetic differs because most intermediate results cannot be represented exactly. After each operation, the hardware rounds the exact mathematical result to the nearest representable value, typically according to IEEE 754 rules. Since regrouping changes which intermediate sums are formed, it also changes where and how rounding occurs.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes or when positive and negative terms nearly cancel. If a small number is added to a much larger one, the small contribution may lie below the available precision and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are accumulated first, however, their combined value may become large enough to affect the later sum. Thus, two mathematically equivalent reduction orders can produce slightly different floating-point answers. Subnormal handling, fused multiply-add instructions, extended intermediate precision, and compiler optimizations can introduce further hardware- or configuration-dependent differences, although the basic cause remains finite precision and rounding.

A matrix multiplication computes every output entry as a dot product: a sequence of multiplications followed by a reduction of the products into one sum. Large matrix multiplications contain enormous numbers of these reductions. High-performance implementations divide the work into tiles and distribute it among vector lanes, processor cores, GPUs, or multiple machines. Partial sums are combined according to schedules chosen for locality and parallel throughput. Those schedules may vary with the library, device, thread count, input shape, kernel selection, or runtime timing.

When the reduction tree changes, the products are added in a different order, so rounding errors accumulate differently. The resulting matrices are usually numerically close but may not be bit-for-bit identical. Small discrepancies can become more noticeable in poorly conditioned calculations or after many dependent operations. Consequently, rerunning a program on another processor, changing parallelism, or selecting a different optimized kernel can alter its final bits even when the inputs and mathematical algorithm are unchanged.

Achieving strict reproducibility therefore requires controlling the reduction order and arithmetic behavior, or using specialized reproducible summation methods. These measures often reduce performance or require extra precision and storage. In most numerical work, reproducibility is instead assessed with tolerances based on expected rounding error rather than exact equality.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of a sum does not change its value: adding the first two numbers and then the third is equivalent to adding the last two and then the first. Floating-point hardware, however, usually rounds the result of each operation to the nearest representable value. Since rounding occurs at intermediate stages, changing the grouping can change what is rounded and therefore change the final result.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes or when positive and negative values nearly cancel. If a very small number is added to a much larger number, the small contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear entirely. If small contributions are combined first, they may accumulate into a value large enough to affect the later addition. Conversely, cancellation can expose rounding errors that were previously insignificant. Thus, two mathematically equivalent addition trees can produce slightly different floating-point answers.

Large matrix multiplication repeatedly computes dot products. Each output entry is a sum of products, often involving thousands or millions of terms. Parallel hardware does not normally add those terms in a single fixed left-to-right sequence. CPUs may divide the work among vector lanes and threads, GPUs may use hierarchical tree reductions across warps and blocks, and distributed systems may combine partial sums according to scheduling and communication patterns. Different library versions, thread counts, matrix shapes, processor architectures, or runtime schedules can therefore select different reduction orders.

Because every partial sum may be rounded, these order changes can alter the low-order bits of each output entry. The discrepancy is usually small relative to the scale of the result, but it can grow with the number of terms and with poorly conditioned data. It can also be amplified by later computations, particularly iterative algorithms, threshold comparisons, or chaotic numerical simulations. Hardware choices such as fused multiply-add instructions, reduced-precision tensor units, extended intermediate precision, and handling of subnormal values can introduce further differences.

Consequently, two matrix multiplications using the same input data and mathematically equivalent algorithms may not be bit-for-bit reproducible. Achieving deterministic results generally requires fixing the reduction order and hardware behavior, often at some performance cost. More demanding reproducibility can require higher-precision accumulation, compensated summation, or specialized exact and reproducible reduction techniques. Numerical software should therefore compare results using error tolerances based on the problem’s scale and conditioning unless exact reproducibility is an explicit requirement.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent most real numbers with finite precision. Under IEEE 754 arithmetic, a floating-point number contains a sign, a fixed-width significand, and an exponent. When two numbers are added, the hardware aligns their significands, computes the sum, and rounds the exact mathematical result to the nearest representable value, usually using round-to-nearest, ties-to-even. Consequently, each addition can discard low-order bits. Changing the placement of parentheses changes when rounding occurs and therefore which information is lost.

For example, suppose a very large positive number is added to a much smaller number. The smaller value may fall below the large number’s available precision and disappear entirely after rounding. If the large number is subsequently canceled by an equally large negative number, the result can be zero. If the two large numbers are canceled first, however, the small value remains. Thus, although real arithmetic guarantees that adding a, b, and c produces the same result regardless of grouping, floating-point evaluations of the two groupings can differ. Cancellation, widely differing magnitudes, overflow, underflow, subnormal handling, and alternative rounding modes can magnify the effect.

A matrix multiplication computes every output element as a dot product: a sequence of products followed by a reduction of their sum. Large implementations rarely add these terms in a single fixed left-to-right order. They divide matrices into tiles, distribute work among vector lanes, processor cores, or accelerators, and combine partial sums using reduction trees. Different thread counts, scheduling decisions, tile sizes, instruction sets, or library versions can therefore produce different reduction orders. Because floating-point addition is non-associative, those mathematically equivalent orders need not produce identical bit patterns.

Fused multiply-add instructions add another complication. They compute a product and an addition with one final rounding, whereas separate multiplication and addition instructions round twice. Fused evaluation is generally more accurate, but it can disagree with an unfused evaluation. Hardware and compiler choices about contraction can therefore affect results even when the apparent algorithm is unchanged.

Usually these discrepancies are tiny, often a few units in the last place, but they can accumulate across long dot products or become prominent in poorly conditioned calculations. They may also influence later comparisons, branching decisions, or iterative algorithms. Reproducibility consequently requires more than using the same input matrices: it may require a deterministic reduction tree, fixed parallelism and kernels, consistent fused-operation behavior, and identical arithmetic settings. Achieving reproducibility across different hardware can demand specialized summation methods or higher precision, often at a performance cost.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with a finite number of bits. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding the first two numbers and then the third is equivalent to adding the last two and then the first. Floating-point hardware, however, usually rounds every result to the nearest representable value. The rounding error introduced at each step depends on the magnitudes and signs of the operands, so changing the grouping can change which information is discarded.

For example, suppose a very large positive value is added to a much smaller value. If the smaller value lies below the available precision at that scale, the rounded result may equal the large value, effectively losing the smaller contribution. If the small value is first combined with another small value, their sum may become large enough to affect the later addition. Cancellation makes this especially visible: adding a large positive number and its negative can expose small terms, whereas adding a small term to one of the large numbers first may erase it before cancellation occurs. Thus, although each individual operation follows a defined rounding rule, different sequences of correctly rounded operations can produce different final answers.

This matters in matrix multiplication because each output entry is a dot product, formed by multiplying corresponding elements and reducing many products into one sum. A simple sequential implementation accumulates these products in a fixed order. Parallel CPUs and GPUs instead divide the work among threads, compute partial sums, and combine those partial sums through reduction trees. Different thread counts, block sizes, vector widths, scheduling decisions, compiler optimizations, or library algorithms can create different reduction orders. Hardware may also use fused multiply-add instructions, which round the product and addition together rather than separately, producing another valid but potentially different result.

For a large matrix multiplication, the discrepancy in any one addition is normally tiny, but thousands or millions of rounded operations can accumulate. Results from two executions may therefore differ in their low-order bits even when both are mathematically correct approximations. Ill-conditioned problems or sums with heavy cancellation can amplify these differences, sometimes enough to affect later comparisons, branching decisions, or iterative algorithms.

Bitwise reproducibility consequently requires more than using the same input values and floating-point format. It generally requires fixing the reduction order and controlling instruction choices, compiler behavior, and library algorithms, often at a performance cost. More accurate summation techniques, higher precision, or reproducible reduction algorithms can reduce or standardize the variation, but ordinary parallel matrix multiplication should not be assumed to produce identical bits across different execution configurations.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding a, b, and c gives the same answer whether a and b are combined first or b and c are combined first. Floating-point hardware, however, must round most intermediate results to the nearest representable value. Different groupings produce different intermediate values, so rounding happens at different points and may discard different information.

This is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. If a small number is added to a much larger one, the small contribution may lie below the available precision and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are added together first, their accumulated value may become large enough to affect the larger number. Cancellation also matters: subtracting nearly equal values can remove leading significant digits and magnify the influence of earlier rounding errors. Thus, although each individual addition usually introduces only a tiny error, the final result can depend on the order in which additions were performed.

Large matrix multiplications contain enormous numbers of such operations. Each output element is a dot product, meaning a sequence of multiplications followed by a reduction that sums all the products. High-performance implementations rarely perform that reduction in one fixed left-to-right order. They divide matrices into tiles, distribute work across processor cores or accelerators, use vector instructions, and combine partial sums through reduction trees. Changing the number of threads, tile dimensions, scheduling decisions, compiler optimizations, hardware architecture, or communication pattern can therefore change the reduction order.

The resulting matrices are usually numerically close, but they need not be bit-for-bit identical. Differences can grow with long reduction chains, poorly scaled inputs, extensive cancellation, or later computations that amplify small perturbations. On GPUs and distributed systems, nondeterministic scheduling or atomic updates may even produce slightly different results between runs on the same machine.

This does not ordinarily mean that the multiplication is incorrect. It means reproducibility must be defined carefully. Numerical reproducibility may accept results within an error tolerance, while bitwise reproducibility requires stricter measures such as deterministic reduction trees, fixed execution settings, higher-precision accumulation, compensated summation, or specially designed reproducible algorithms. Those measures often cost performance because they restrict parallel execution or require additional computation and storage. Consequently, fast matrix multiplication and exact run-to-run identity can be competing goals, even when every execution follows the floating-point standard correctly.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding a, b, and c as (a + b) + c is equivalent to a + (b + c). Floating-point hardware, however, must round most intermediate results to the nearest representable value. Since rounding occurs after each operation, changing which operands are combined first can change what information is discarded and therefore change the final result.

The effect is especially visible when operands have very different magnitudes. If a very small number is added to a very large number, the small contribution may lie below the precision available at the large number’s scale and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are added together first, their accumulated value may become large enough to affect the later addition. Cancellation also matters: adding nearly opposite values can expose rounding errors that were previously insignificant. IEEE 754 specifies floating-point formats and rounding behavior, but it does not make addition associative; correctly rounded individual operations can still produce different correctly computed results for different groupings.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products. Each output element is a sum of products, often involving thousands or millions of terms. A straightforward implementation might accumulate those terms from left to right, but optimized implementations rarely use that exact order. CPUs may use vector instructions and multiple partial accumulators. GPUs divide work among threads, warps, and blocks, then combine partial sums through tree reductions. Distributed systems partition matrices across machines and merge results according to communication schedules. Libraries may also select different kernels based on hardware, matrix shape, thread count, or available memory. Fused multiply-add instructions and reduced-precision tensor hardware can introduce further differences by changing where rounding occurs or how much precision intermediate values retain.

Consequently, two matrix multiplications using mathematically identical inputs can produce slightly different output entries when their reduction orders differ. The discrepancies are usually a few units in the last place, but they can grow for long, poorly conditioned sums or propagate through subsequent computations. Parallel execution can make the issue more visible if scheduling changes the order in which partial results are combined.

Reproducibility therefore requires more than fixing inputs and random seeds. It may require a deterministic kernel, fixed thread and partition configurations, consistent compiler and hardware settings, and an explicitly controlled reduction scheme. Stronger approaches use higher-precision accumulation, compensated summation, or reproducible summation algorithms, although these generally cost performance. In many applications, results should be compared with suitable numerical tolerances rather than exact bitwise equality.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In ordinary arithmetic, changing parentheses does not change a sum: adding a and b first, then c, gives the same result as adding b and c first, then a. A floating-point processor, however, usually rounds the result of every operation to the nearest representable value in a format such as IEEE 754 binary32 or binary64. Since the spacing between representable values grows with magnitude, adding a small number to a much larger one may have no visible effect: the small contribution can be rounded away. If smaller terms are combined first, their accumulated value may become large enough to affect the final result. Consequently, the two parenthesizations can produce different bit patterns.

Other hardware details can amplify or alter these differences. Fused multiply-add instructions compute a product and an addition with only one final rounding, whereas separate multiplication and addition normally round twice. CPUs and GPUs may choose different instructions, intermediate precisions, treatments of subnormal numbers, or compiler transformations. These choices generally comply with the relevant floating-point rules, yet they need not produce identical results. The discrepancy is usually tiny, but it can become significant when many operations accumulate rounding error or when the calculation is poorly conditioned.

Each entry of a matrix product is a dot product: a sequence of products followed by a reduction that adds them together. Large matrix multiplications rarely perform that reduction in a simple left-to-right order. High-performance implementations divide matrices into tiles, distribute work among vector lanes, cores, threads, or GPU blocks, and combine partial sums through reduction trees. The selected order can depend on the library, processor, thread count, tile size, scheduling decisions, or autotuning results. Two executions that use different reduction orders can therefore round at different intermediate points and return slightly different entries, even when their mathematical inputs are identical.

These small entrywise changes may propagate into later computations, particularly iterative algorithms, threshold comparisons, decompositions, or systems near numerical singularity. Thus numerical reproducibility must be distinguished from bitwise reproducibility: results may agree within a sensible error tolerance without matching bit for bit. Exact repeatability requires controlling the algorithm, instruction choices, thread scheduling, and reduction order, often at a performance cost. Higher precision, pairwise or compensated summation, and specialized reproducible linear-algebra libraries can reduce variability, but ordinary parallel matrix multiplication should not be assumed to produce identical bits across different hardware configurations or execution strategies.

Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of a sum does not change its value: adding the first two numbers and then the third is equivalent to adding the first number to the sum of the other two. Floating-point arithmetic breaks this rule because most real numbers cannot be represented exactly. After nearly every addition, the exact result must be rounded to the nearest representable value, typically according to the IEEE 754 standard. Different groupings create different intermediate values, so rounding occurs at different points and may produce different final results.

The effect is especially visible when numbers vary greatly in magnitude or when positive and negative terms nearly cancel. If a very small number is added to a much larger one, the small contribution may fall below the available precision and disappear entirely. If small terms are combined first, however, they may accumulate into a value large enough to affect the result. Similarly, cancellation can expose rounding errors that were insignificant before subtraction. Hardware features such as fused multiply-add can improve accuracy by performing a multiplication and addition with only one final rounding, but they do not restore associativity. Differences in precision, compiler optimization, and instruction selection can introduce further variation.

Large matrix multiplication repeatedly computes dot products, each of which is a reduction over many products. Mathematically, the order of summation is irrelevant. On real machines, the reduction order determines the sequence of intermediate floating-point values and therefore the rounding history. A serial implementation might accumulate terms from left to right. A vectorized implementation may sum several independent lanes and combine them afterward. A multithreaded CPU or GPU may divide the work among many workers and reduce partial sums through a tree whose shape depends on block sizes, scheduling, kernel choice, or device architecture. Optimized libraries may also change their algorithms according to matrix dimensions and available hardware.

Consequently, two mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications can produce entries that differ by a few units in the last place, and ill-conditioned calculations may amplify those discrepancies. Results are usually numerically close but not bit-for-bit identical. Reproducibility therefore requires more than using the same inputs: it may require fixing the algorithm, hardware, thread count, compiler settings, library version, and reduction order. Deterministic kernels can stabilize the order, while compensated or higher-precision summation can reduce sensitivity. Tests should generally use justified numerical tolerances rather than exact equality unless strict deterministic execution is explicitly guaranteed.

Floating-point arithmetic cannot usually store the exact result of each operation, however. After every addition, the hardware rounds the mathematical result to the nearest representable value according to the active rounding mode. If small values are combined first, their accumulated sum may become large enough to affect the larger value. Similarly, cancellation can discard leading significant digits and magnify the influence of rounding in later operations. Thus, two reduction orders can use exactly the same inputs and perform mathematically equivalent work while producing slightly different floating-point results. Features such as fused multiply-add, extended intermediate precision, and the handling of subnormal values can introduce additional differences across processors or compiler settings.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products. Each output element is a sum of products, often involving thousands or millions of terms. High-performance implementations divide this work into blocks and execute them across vector lanes, CPU threads, GPU warps, or multiple devices. The partial sums are then reduced through a tree whose order depends on the algorithm, tile dimensions, thread scheduling, hardware architecture, and communication pattern. Changing any of these can change the sequence of roundings. Even if each discrepancy is tiny, errors can accumulate, and cancellation or ill-conditioned data can make the observed differences much larger.

Consequently, parallel matrix multiplication is often numerically consistent without being bit-for-bit reproducible. Repeating a computation with a deterministic implementation on identical hardware may produce identical bits, but changing thread counts, libraries, devices, or reduction strategies may alter low-order digits. These differences can propagate through later computations and occasionally affect convergence tests, comparisons, or discrete decisions. Reproducibility therefore requires more than fixing the input and random seed. It may require deterministic reduction trees, controlled compiler and hardware settings, higher-precision accumulation, or specialized reproducible summation methods. Such measures usually cost performance, memory, or portability, so numerical software commonly validates results with tolerances instead of demanding exact equality.
